passage: Ishita, sit. Suresh was sixteen once and had two doors in front of me: a coaching class that promised a good rank, or a music course with a teacher I liked. Everyone said rank. So I took a sheet of paper and wrote first, not the names of the courses, but what I wanted from my life: to make things, and to decide my own days. Creativity. Independence. Then I put each course beside those two words. Coaching gave me a timetable made by someone else. Music gave me a violin and a choice. I showed the page to Papa and Ma at dinner. Papa said, "Good. Now let's check whether the fees and the travel are workable." Ma asked me to try one month of music first. We agreed. The list did not choose for me. It showed me what I was choosing.

qa.q: Which two values did Suresh write on the page?
What did Suresh want from life, according to the story?
qa.a: Suresh wanted to make things and to decide the days, which is why a timetable made by someone else felt wrong.

qa.q: Which step in the story made the choice clearer, and why?
qa.a: Writing the values before naming the courses let Suresh hold each course up against them.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt about trying one month of music first?
qa.a: Ma may have felt cautious but supportive, wanting Suresh to try the music course while keeping a chance to review it.

grounding: Shows a student naming what matters before choosing between a coaching class and a music course, with parents' input.

passage: The coaching form had to be submitted by midnight, and the night bus to Pune had one bar of signal. Vishal held his phone up to the window and sighed. Two tabs were open: the rank coaching centre his cousins had joined, and a year-long music production course. His sister Anjali, sitting beside him, asked, "Which one, then?" "I don't know. Everyone says coaching." He opened his notes app and typed: What do I care about? He wrote: making things of my own. Deciding my own hours. He stared at it. "Coaching is six days a week, all fixed. The music course lets me build my own tracks." Anjali said, "Call Mummy and Papa before the signal drops." He did. Papa asked, "Can you still keep up with school?" Vishal said yes. They agreed. He filled the music form at 11:40.

qa.q: At what time did Vishal fill the music form?
What does Vishal writing 'making things of my own' suggest about what he wants?
qa.a: It suggests he feels most alive being creative and independent, and would feel boxed in by six fixed days of coaching.

qa.q: Which approach helped Vishal most, and why?
qa.a: Naming what he cares about before choosing; once creativity and freedom were written down, the music course clearly fit better.

qa.q: How might Vishal's parents see his reasons?
qa.a: They seem reassured because he explained his values and promised to keep up with school, so they could agree with confidence.

grounding: A teen facing a deadline names his values, creativity and independence, then chooses the music course with his parents' input.

subtype: Approach: names what matters before choosing a path [Thinking]
passage: In their flat in Andheri, Chinmay spread two brochures on the dining table: a rank coaching centre and a weekend course in Carnatic violin with his teacher, Jomon Sir. His parents sat across from him. "Before you pick," Amma said, "tell us what matters to you." Chinmay took a pencil and thought aloud. "I like making up my own tunes. I like working things out without someone checking every hour. Coaching is timetables and mock tests. That's the opposite." Appa frowned. "And your engineering entrance?" Chinmay nodded. "I'll do self-study for maths with the online test series, and ask you to check my scores every Sunday." His parents looked at each other. "The violin course, then. But Sundays we check," Appa said. Chinmay wrote "Sunday check" at the top of his list.

qa.q: What was the weekend course Chinmay was considering?
qa.a: A weekend course in Carnatic violin with his teacher, Jomon Sir.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel about coaching, judging from what he says?
qa.a: He seems uneasy about it, feeling it would be the opposite of the creativity and independence he values.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do if the Sunday checks show he's slipping in maths?
qa.a: He could add a short daily maths slot or talk with his parents about extra help, without giving up what he values.

qa.q: How do Chinmay's parents see his plan?
qa.a: They are cautious but willing, and feel easier once he offers weekly score checks.

grounding: A teen names creativity and independence as what he values and chooses a course accordingly with his parents' input.
